title: Brisbane – Queensland/Australia
intro:
Welcome to my 1st blog article, where we journey through the vibrant coffee culture of Brisbane.

If you’ve ever found yourself longing for that perfect cup of Joe while basking in the warm Australian sunshine, then you’re in the right place.

In this series, I’ll be your guide through Brisbane's bustling coffee scene, uncovering hidden gems and must-visit spots.

So, grab your cup, settle in, and let's dive into the rich and aromatic world of Brisbane’s coffee culture.

content.subtitle: Industry Beans – Newstead
content.text:
Nestled in the heart of Newstead, Industry Beans is a must-visit for coffee enthusiasts.

Known for roasting their beans in small batches, this cafe boasts three roasteries across Australia, each with its unique espresso blend.

Whether you’re a seasoned coffee lover or a curious newcomer, Industry Beans provides a refined and memorable coffee experience.

content.subtitle: Edward Cafe – Brisbane CBD
content.text:
Situated in the bustling Central Business District, Edward Cafe is a gem for both coffee lovers and foodies alike.

Besides serving outstanding coffee, this cafe offers delicious sandwiches that make for a perfect lunch break or mid-afternoon snack.

The friendly atmosphere and prime location make it an ideal spot to unwind and indulge in some of Brisbane’s finest brews and bites.

content.subtitle: Bear Bones Coffee – Fortitude Valley
content.text:
A visit to Bear Bones Coffee in Fortitude Valley is a must for those who appreciate the art of coffee roasting.

In the summer months, they roast their beans early in the morning before the heat sets in, ensuring the freshest flavours.

One of the highlights at Bear Bones is the Barista Breakfast, which includes an espresso, a batch brew, and a flat white.

The batch brew from Honduras is a sensation, while the Papua New Guinea espresso is remarkably fruity and complex.

meta.title: Five Cups, four days in Adelaide
meta.intro: From the East End to Glenelg, Port Adelaide to Soho — a week of chasing extraordinary cups across the city.

stops.pull_quote: The food earns its place alongside the coffee — that's rare.
stops.body: You start here. You always start here. Exchange has held its own as one of the city's finest for over a decade — ranked 37th in the World's 100 Best Coffee Shops in its inaugural year. The Turkish Eggs arrived first: poached eggs over whipped yoghurt, charred broccolini, grilled sourdough, dukkah and chilli oil. Produce-driven, well-considered. The filter was an Ecuador Single Origin from the Hakuna Matata region — Typica, Washed, Light roast, 1350 masl. Cranberry acidity present but never pushy. Clean, bright, deeply reliable.

stops.pull_quote: Ember sources with intention. That card on the table isn't decoration.
stops.body: Ember is doing something different. The fit-out is spare and considered — clean lines, natural light, the energy of a place that takes itself seriously without being precious about it. The espresso was a Rafael Vinhal LOT456 — Catuai & Icatu from Vinhal Farm in Cerrado Mineiro, Anaerobic Natural, SCA 86. Presented on a card at the table. The coconut note was unmistakable — not added, not milk-based, just what the bean does. Wrapped in milk chocolate and vanilla sweetness, one of the most complete espressos of the week.

stops.pull_quote: Sometimes the straightforward cup is the most satisfying one of the week.
stops.body: Port Adelaide doesn't get enough credit. The Dutchman is a proper neighbourhood café doing proper coffee — no theatre, no fuss. The double-shot flat white arrived with a tulip pour that looked too good to drink. Didn't hesitate anyway. The milk texture was exceptional — silky microfoam that integrates completely. The espresso underneath punched through with full body and a clean finish.

stops.pull_quote: A lot of care and distance between a farm in Kayanza and your table by the beach.
stops.body: Glenelg doesn't feel like a specialty coffee destination — which is exactly why Closer is such a find. Glen and Sunny run this place, and they are genuinely two of the nicest people you'll meet behind a bar. The kind of hospitality that feels effortless because it actually is. And Closer is just one part of their world — they also run a record store and a hair salon. Culture, community, coffee, all under one roof. The Burundi Mutana from the Long Miles Project, served on a steel tray with a glass server, a ceramic cup, and a glass information tube with the full origin story. As the cup cooled, strawberry and blueberry came forward unmistakably. Done well.

stops.pull_quote: Wait for it to cool. That's when the sugar cane notes come forward properly.
stops.body: The week ends here — and Soho earns the closer. What makes it special isn't just the coffee in the cup — it's that they roast their own. The Phantom Series machine out the back, Hot Donna, is doing serious work. Watching a batch tumble into the cooling tray puts everything in perspective. Kenya Single Origin, three-stage pour: 50ml bloom, up to 100ml, then the rest. The acidity was beautifully balanced — bright, structured, with sugar cane emerging properly as the cup cooled.
